Part 1 · Alevism2 min

Who are the Alevis? Demographics and roots

15–20%

of Turkey’s population (estimates), the country’s largest non-Sunni minority: an umbrella term for diverse regional and tribal communities with an esoteric, Ali-centred worldview.

Turkish · about ⅔
Iranian · about ⅓

The Iranian-language third speaks Kurmanji (Kurdish) and Zazaki, both Northwestern Iranian.

Alevis at a public gathering · video still, “Who Are the Alevis?”
c. 1501

Qizilbash (“Red Heads”)

Turkmen and Iranian followers of the Safawiyya Sufi order and Shah Ismail, founder of the Safavid Empire.

Ottoman period

Persecution as heretics

Qizilbash revolts were suppressed; communities were labelled heretics (rafidi, zindiq).

Centuries of retreat

Secrecy and taqiyya

Remote mountain villages, strict endogamy, and ritual preserved in secret.

Early 20th century

“Alevi” becomes the name

Adopted gradually to move away from the loaded label Qizilbash (Dressler, 2008).

Dressler, “Alevis”, EI3 (2008)

Part 1 · Alevism4 min · click a card to open it

Esoteric cosmology: four pillars of Alevism

Inner over outer

An inner (batin) reading of Islam that downplays outward (zahir) duties.

No five daily prayers, no mosque, no Ramadan fast, no pilgrimage to Mecca. The human heart is the real Ka‘ba.

The Speaking Quran

The Quran is recognised, yet plays a marginal role in daily ritual.

A saying ascribed to Ali: “I am the speaking Quran” (konuşan Kuran benim). The living guide speaks where the written book cannot.

One light: Allah, Muhammad, Ali

Muhammad and Ali were created from one divine light before mankind.

In the Kırklar Cemi myth, Muhammad meets thirty-nine saints led by Ali during his heavenly ascent: wilaya (sainthood) outranks nubuwwa (prophethood).

The Four Gates (Dört Kapı)

A path from outer law to Divine Truth.

Şeriat
Tarikat
Marifet
Hakikat
Outer law → mystical path → inner gnosis → Divine Truth.
Eline, diline, beline sahip ola maxim attributed to Hacı Bektaş Veli
Handno theft, no violence
Tongueno lying
Loinsfidelity
Core ethics, which scholars such as Irène Mélikoff link to Manichaean roots.
Based on Dressler (EI3, 2008) and Sökefeld (2004)
Part 1 · Alevism2 min · step through the rows

Alevism versus Twelver Shia Islam

Alevis share a deep reverence for Ali and the Twelve Imams, yet stand outside formal Shia jurisprudence and clerical authority.

Twelver Shia IslamAnatolian Alevism
Religious authorityFormally trained jurists (Marja‘-e Taqlid)Hereditary spiritual leaders (Dedes) from sacred lineages (Ocaks)
Legal frameworkDetailed jurisprudence (Sharia, fiqh) from Quran and HadithEsoteric moral code (Batin); outward Sharia is only the first gate
Primary sourcesArabic Quran and canonical Shia Hadith collectionsOral tradition (Nefes poetry with Saz) and Turkish Buyruk texts (16th c.)
Worship and spaceFive daily prayers in a mosque; Ramadan fast; Hajj to MeccaCem in a Cemevi; 12-day Muharram fast; the human heart as Ka‘ba
View of the QuranCentral liturgical scripture, interpreted by juristsMarginal in ritual; Ali venerated as the living “Speaking Quran”

Social structure: Ocak, Dede, and Musahiplik

Muhammad and Ali
→
The 12 Imams
→
Ocaksacred lineage, “hearth”
→
Dedes / Seyyidshereditary leaders
→
Talipslay disciples
The chain begins here

The Twelve Imams in a popular devotional poster: Alevi lineages trace their sanctity back through them.

Image © akg-images
Dede and Talip

A hereditary bond

  • Dedes claim descent from the Prophet’s family (Seyyids) and act as ritual leaders, teachers and mediators.
  • Each Talip family is bound by descent to a specific Ocak; historically rural and endogamous.
Musahiplik · companionship
♂♀♂♀
  • A lifelong pact between two married couples, modelled on Muhammad and Ali.
  • Mutual spiritual and material duty, stronger than blood ties; their children may not intermarry.
Oral memory and texts
  • Bards (Asıks) sing Nefes hymns on the Saz, the “Quran with strings”.
  • Buyruk manuals (16th c.) stayed secret in Dede families until the mid-20th century.

Part 1 · Alevism3 min · five stages

The Cem: “the prayer of Alevis is cem”

Men and women sit as equals in a circle led by the Dede

Five stages of worship

Step through the stages. Reconciliation comes first, then hymn, myth, ritual turning and shared food. The twelve-day Matem Orucu fast in Muharram mourns Karbala.

Stage 1 · Görgü

Mandatory reconciliation

All disputes must be settled before the Dede before worship begins. In a mosque, by contrast, enemies may pray side by side.

Stage 2 · Oniki Hizmet

Twelve services and hymns

Twelve symbolic duties, among them the Dede, the musician (Zakir), the candle-keeper and the watchman. The Zakir plays the Saz and sings Nefes hymns.

Stage 3 · Kırklar Cemi

The Gathering of the Forty

Ritual re-enactment of Muhammad’s heavenly meeting with thirty-nine saints led by Ali, affirming wilaya over nubuwwa.

Stage 4 · Semah

The flight of the crane

Men and women turn together, imitating the sacred crane (turna) and the cycle of the universe.

Stage 5 · Lokma

The communal meal

Offerings brought by every family are blessed and shared equally, reinforcing solidarity.

UNESCO: Semah, Alevi-Bektaşi ritualOfficial UNESCO film · show 1–1.5 min↗ Sunni or Shia? Who Are the Alevis?Documentary · opens at 30:39↗
From secrecy to public identity. Urbanisation and the 1989 Alevi revival in Germany broke centuries of taqiyya and made the Cem a public marker of identity (Sökefeld, 2004). Our question: why did the Figure of Ali reach such cosmic status?
Photos: stills from “Sunni or Shia? Who Are the Alevis?” (YouTube)

Part 2 · Enigmas and Method6 min · step through the enigmas

Four historical enigmas surrounding Ali

1

Unmatched devotion

Over 300 million believers (Twelvers, Ismailis, Zaydis, Alevis, Alawites, Yarsan, Sunni Sufis) revere Ali. Caliph Umar, architect of the Arab Empire, never inspired a spiritual cult.

2

Absent from the conquests

A legendary warrior in Muhammad’s lifetime, yet absent from every early Arab war of conquest after the Prophet’s death.

3

The capital moves to Kufa

Ali moved the capital from Medina to Kufa in Sasanian Iraq, beside al-Hira, an old hub of Eastern Christian, Gnostic and Manichaean traditions.

4

A divine name

Early Shiite texts link the name “Ali” (“The Most High”) to one of the supreme Names of God.

Schematic map, approximate positions. Step 3 shows the move from Medina to Kufa.

Amir-Moezzi, Ali, le secret bien gardé (2020)
Part 2 · Enigmas and Method7 min

From the “Historical Ali” to the “Figure of Ali”

Ali stands at the centre of three inseparable crises, and every source about him is partisan. So Amir-Moezzi studies the Figure of Ali: how the earliest texts represent him.

The method: read the sources from before the rationalist turn
to c. 950Qumm school

Early esoteric, “non-rational” tradition

Hadith compilers record the cosmic Ali: pre-existent light, secret knowledge, the Speaking Quran.

Basa’ir al-darajat · al-Saffar al-Qummi, d. 903al-Kafi · al-Kulayni, d. 941
945The Buyids take Baghdad; Shiite scholars gain court patronage
late 10th c. onBaghdad school

Rationalist theological-legal tradition

al-Mufid (d. 1022), al-Sharif al-Murtada (d. 1044) and al-Tusi (d. 1067), close to Mu‘tazilite rationalism, push the esoteric material aside.

Deconstructing ghuluww. The line between “moderate” and “extremist” Shiism is a later, artificial construct: bold cosmic beliefs about Ali already stand inside foundational Twelver hadith collections.
Amir-Moezzi (1994, 2011, 2020)
Part 3 · Worldview of Din Ali8 min · peel the shell

A two-layered world: manifest and hidden

Outer dimension · manifest

Zahirظاهر

MessengerThe Prophet brings universal law for the public.
Mode of scripture · TanzilThe literal, revealed text.
The Silent QuranWritten words cannot speak for themselves.
LimitWithout Batin, the outer form is a lifeless shell.
Inseparableshell and kernel · body and spirit
Inner dimension · esoteric

Batinباطن

GuideThe Imam (Wali, Ali) leads the initiated to inner reality.
Mode of scripture · Ta’wilSpiritual decoding back to the origin.
The Speaking QuranAli, living word of God, echoed in Alevism today.
NecessityWithout Zahir, inner truth has no anchor in this world.

The Warrior of Ta’wil. As Muhammad fought for the tanzil, Ali fights for the ta’wil: Siffin seen as a defence of the Quran’s spirit.

The Mushaf of Ali. Pre-Buyid Shiite texts held that the Uthmanic codex was altered, while Ali kept the complete Quran with its commentary.

Amir-Moezzi, The Divine Guide in Early Shi‘ism (1994)
Part 3 · Worldview of Din Ali8 min

Cosmic dualism and the “Religion of Ali”

Armies of Sacred Intellect

the Imam and his followers
vs.

Armies of Ignorance

his enemies

In al-Kafi, history is a cosmic war that began before physical creation: 75 armies against 75.

Pillar one

Walayaولاية

Sacred love, loyalty and spiritual alliance with the Imam.

Pillar two

Bara’aبراءة

Sacred dissociation from the enemies of the Imam.

Neutrality is impossible in a dualistic universe; faith needs both poles.

The historical phrase

Din Ali, “the Religion of Ali”

Early chroniclers such as al-Tabari record it, used by Ali’s supporters and opponents alike.

Sunnaof Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman
Dinof Ali, the only figure after Muhammad whose name is joined to “religion”

A distinct faith rooted in devotion to the Prophet’s family (Ahl al-Bayt), in tension with the “Religion of the Empire”.

Din Ali
esoteric, centred on the Prophet’s family
Religion of the Empire
official Islam of Umayyads and Abbasids
Amir-Moezzi (2020), after al-Kulayni and al-Tabari
Part 3 · Worldview of Din Ali7 min · four stages

From “Ali the Messiah” to the “Luminous Imam”

Premise 1The oldest Quranic layers announce the imminent end of the world (the Hour).
+
Premise 2In a biblical, Judeo-Christian environment, the end of time needs an apocalyptic Saviour or Messiah.
⇒
Amir-Moezzi’s thesisEarly Shiism cast Ali as the Messiah and Judge of the Last Day.
1
Apocalyptic urgency

The Hour is near

Announcing the End required a saviour figure in a Late Antique Judeo-Christian world.

2
Paraclete and Messiah

The “Second Christ”

Muhammad is linked to the Paraclete; the oldest Shiite sermons portray Ali as the Second Christ and Judge. The title al-Faruq (Syriac Paruqa, Saviour) first belonged to Ali.

3
De-messianisation

The world did not end

As the Umayyad Empire consolidated under Abd al-Malik, the state suppressed apocalyptic urgency and canonised scripture.

4
The Luminous Imam

Theophany

God’s Essence stays unknowable; His Names and Attributes appear in the Imam. Ali’s dual nature: nasut (humanity) and lahut (divinity).

Amir-Moezzi, Ali, le secret bien gardé (2020)

Part 4 · Ali’s Family and the Branches14 min · click a branch

Evolution of Shiism: from Ali’s charisma to five branches

After Ali and Karbala

Two questions split the followers

  • Who is the rightful Imam?
  • Is the Imamate political, or cosmic?
Click a branch above, or press → to step through. The map shows where each branch left its mark.
Late 7th century

Kaysaniyya

Birth of Mahdism
  • Formed around Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, a son of Ali.
  • Introduced Occultation (ghayba), Return (raj‘a) and the Promised Mahdi.
Legacy: messianic return
8th century to today

Zaydiyya

Political revolt
  • Rejected taqiyya; armed revolt against tyranny.
  • Any learned, brave descendant of Fatima who rises can lead.
Legacy: Yemen today
8th century to today

Ismailiyya

Institutional Batin
  • Institutionalised batin and philosophical ta’wil.
  • Built the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt and Alamut in Iran.
Legacy: Bohras and Nizaris (Aga Khan)
10th century to today

Twelvers (Imamiyya)

The jurisprudential turn
  • After the Occultation, early esotericism gave way to law and rationalism.
  • Safavid state religion in 1501, first powered by the Qizilbash.
Legacy: Iran, Iraq, Lebanon
Medieval to today

Esoteric movements

Beyond outward Sharia
  • Kept the luminous, cosmic Ali: Nusayris (Alawites), Druze, Anatolian Alevis and Bektashis, Yarsan (Ahl-e Haqq).
  • Ottoman records lumped them as ghulat; Mir-Hosseini shows their living “Inner Truth”.
Charisma of Ali
7th c.→Esoteric core
pre-Buyid Qumm→Buyid rationalism,
Fatimid empire→Safavid state,
living minorities

Conclusion3 min, then 7 min discussion

Answering the opening enigma

Ali endures across centuries and sectarian borders not because of a brief political caliphate, but because of the spiritual, esoteric and cosmic Figure of Ali.

Through the Speaking Quran, Din Ali, the Alid lineages and living mystical music, Ali has been the centre of gravity of Islamic esotericism, and a contested one.

Esmail Jalayer, Qajar period
